utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-47-PT, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Would the accused be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated. Could we have the appearances again, please. For the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, again; good morning, Defence counsel. Again for the Prosecution appear Mr. David Re, trial attorney, on my right-hand side; Ms. Kimberly Fleming, case manager, on my left-hand side; and I, Ekkehard Withopf, Senior Trial Attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Defence for Mr. Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, attorney from Sarajevo; my colleague Mr. Stephane Bourgon, an attorney from Montreal; and our legal assistant Mirna Milanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, Mr. Rodney Dixon, and our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the accused stand, please. Mr. Hadzihasanovic, could you introduce yourself, tell us your identity, your name. THE ACCUSED HADZIHASANOVIC: [Interpretation] My name is Enver Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your date of birth, please. THE ACCUSED HADZIHASANOVIC: [Interpretation] I was born on the 7th of July, 1950 in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your address? THE ACCUSED HADZIHASANOVIC: [Interpretation] I now live in Sarajevo, in Trampina Street number 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your profession? THE ACCUSED HADZIHASANOVIC: [Interpretation] By profession I was a general of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Since 2000 I am a pensioner. I retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Kubura, would you please introduce yourself once again. THE ACCUSED KUBURA: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Amir Kubura, born on the 4th of March, 1964 in Kakanj. I am living in Sarajevo, Topalosman-Pase Street number 22, an officer of the army of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated. This Pre-Trial Conference, pursuant to Rule 73 bis of the Rules of Procedure, has an agenda which is as follows: The Chamber must, following indications from the Prosecution determine the number of witnesses that 3 they intend to call, protective measures that may be required for some of the witnesses, the order in which the witnesses are going to appear, the duration of the testimony of each witness, the estimated length of testimony, the number of witness statements and transcripts of prior testimony pursuant to Rule 92 bis of the Rules, to possibly indicate the timetable proposed for the submission of documents. The Chamber also needs to be informed regarding the current status with respect to the disclosure of documents pursuant to Rule 66(A) of the Rules, also to inform the Chamber of the progress made in translating the documents into one of the working languages of the Tribunal, and to indicate where we stand regarding the disclosure of exculpatory material pursuant to Rule 68 of the Rules. The Chamber now consists of one Judge only due to the fact that 66 ter (C) and 73 bis of the Rules allow the Pre-Trial Judge to be alone during the Pre-Trial Conference. Before giving the floor to the Prosecution regarding the various items of the agenda, I should like to address the question regarding the problem of agreement on points of fact and law pursuant to Rule 66 ter (H). During the last Status Conference, I asked the parties to communicate and to tell the Chamber in writing which are the points of law and fact on which an agreement had been reached or which are in dispute, and this morning the Chamber received a motion from the Prosecution concerning the difficulties encountered in this procedure due to the fact that the Defence for Mr. Kubura did not produce any document. I would like to recall that the Prosecutor provided a list of facts. These points were provided to the parties. The Defence counsel for Mr. Hadzihasanovic did respond in writing, indicating that it would agree on points -- on certain points as well as series B, series C, and series F, points 3 and 12, for series H points 32 and 34, and J point 1. On the other hand, the Defence also produced a document to the Prosecution regarding the points on which the Prosecution should agree, but the Prosecution indicated that the points mentioned are not directly related to the facts submitted to the Chamber. That is where we stand for the moment. And regarding the points of agreement and disagreement, I should like first to give the floor to the Prosecution, after which I will give the floor to the Defence. Mr. Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the issue of stipulations is a very, very serious one and it will have a very serious impact on the proceedings in this trial. You are referring to the two filings, to the detailed submissions in the two filings of this week, namely the Prosecution's notice to the Trial Chamber concerning the lack of agreement and, number 2, the motion requesting the Pre-Trial Judge to order Defence counsel to file submissions pursuant to Rule 65 ter (H). The facts have in great detail been outlined in the filings. They speak for themselves. The Prosecution has come to the view that the Defence, quite contrary to their repeated announcements, is not willing, not willing to confine the issues litigated. There is no reason for the Prosecution to litigate to the Defence proposed submissions. Almost all facts, almost all of the proposed facts are quotes from the Blaskic and from the Kordic and Cerkez Trial Chamber judgement, a few ones from the Kupreskic judgement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: They in great detail describe the crimes committed by the HVO against the Muslim population in Central Bosnia. Such proposed stipulations indicate the Defence may raise a defence based on the tu quoque or reprisal principle. The Tribunal's jurisprudence is quite clear in that respect. Neither the principles of tu quoque nor reprisals constitute a defence. Such a defence has no basis in the law. The Prosecution does not stipulate to the Defence proposed admissions beyond the few ones the Prosecution did for a number of reasons. Number one, because such proposed submissions stipulate to factual findings from other cases that are not in issue in this case, meaning that they cannot have any bearing on the resolution of this case. Stipulations would be meaningless. Number two, such factual findings are irrelevant to the third amended indictment; and even more important, number three, such factual findings are currently under appeal. My colleague Mr. Re will now continue to detail any further issues and to detail the result the current situation may, and probably will have, on the further proceedings. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution is gravely concerned at the lack of agreement between the parties despite the Prosecution's earnest, earnest endeavours over the last month to obtain some agreement as to the issues which should not be in dispute in a case which is purely based upon command responsibility, that is, the liability of the accused for the acts under 7 -- Article 7(3). It is for this reason the Prosecution has filed two documents in the last week; firstly, the notice to the Trial Chamber setting out the situation and attaching the two proposals from both sides, and following the breakdown, so to speak, of talks between the two parties, an exhortation to the Trial Chamber to intervene and to order the Defence to file written submissions pursuant to Rule 65 ter (H) as to basically why they will not stipulate to matters which in the Prosecution's submissions simply should not be in dispute in this trial. The Prosecution, pursuant to talks with the Defence which have been going for some time over the last few months and which the Prosecution and the Defence addressed in a 65 ter conference many months ago, the Prosecution provided the Defence with an advanced copy of its pre-trial brief in the first week of September, which was almost five weeks before we filed our full pre-trial brief. The Defence have been on notice for over two years as to, in broad terms, the case against the two accused, and over the past two years, the Defence -- the Prosecution has served on the Defence thousands of documents, including our 1.200 or so proposed exhibits. The indictment has been amended several times. It's got smaller, with the exception of the Miletici allegation against Mr. Kubura, but the evidence was -- or the allegation was already there. The Prosecution says there is no reason why the Defence should not be able to stipulate to some of the most basic issues which are -- which should not be litigated in this trial. If Your Honour looks at the document which the Prosecution filed, and the Defence response, Your Honour will notice a -- the response of the accused Hadzihasanovic, Your Honour will note that the agreement so far seems to be entirely random. The Defence will stipulate to some matters, some personal matters in relation to both accused, the Defence will stipulate in the series which the Prosecution outlined of the A series, which is those relating to Mr. Hadzihasanovic. The Defence will stipulate to A.1, 2, 3, 6, and 8. Now, this is significant in the terms of what's happening. 8 is on the 14th of November, 1992, Enver Hadzihasanovic was made the commander of the 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Flowing from that, under international law, a person in the accused's position assumes certain responsibilities. The Prosecution has outlined three of those in A.17, A.18, and A.19. A.17 is at all times relevant to this indictment. Enver Hadzihasanovic was required to abide by the laws and customs governing the conduct of armed conflicts, including the Geneva Conventions of 1949 and the Additional Protocols thereto. A.18, that the accused Enver Hadzihasanovic was responsible for ensuring that military units under his command and effective control respected and applied these international rules -- these rules of international law. And 19, that he was obliged by superior order to initiate proceedings for legal sanctions against individuals under his command and effective control who had violated the International Law of War. In the Prosecution's respectful submission, Your Honour, those three things we have asked the Defence to stipulate to are no more than a statement of international humanitarian law, yet three weeks after the Defence has had our fairly detailed proposals which are based only upon the indictment, the pre-trial brief, and the evidence we have served over the last two years, they cannot even stipulate to those three most basic features which must flow from a stipulation to A8. If you are the commander, you must assume the responsibilities in 17, 18, and 19. The Prosecution, quite frankly, Your Honour, is mystified as to why so long after we filed or gave them a copy of the pre-trial brief, an advance copy, and gave this lengthy document which is divided down line by line to enable the Defence to consider each separate thing. One thing leads to another. How far will you go? Well, the Defence won't even go to, as we say in colloquial terms, first base. That is, for example, that the 3rd Corps had a certain structure. The Defence so far will stipulate to nothing relating to the structure of the 3rd Corps, not even to the fact of the establishment of the 3rd Corps by government decree. They will stipulate to nothing relating to government regulations or decrees, which are things the Tribunal could take judicial notice of. The Prosecution has to ask: What is going on? Why, on the day of the Pre-Trial Conference, four days before the trial commences, are we in this situation? Which brings me to the ramifications. The failure of the Defence to agree to the most basic of the stipulations has left the Prosecution and the pre-trial -- Your Honour and the Chamber in an invidious situation. We don't know what evidence we have to call to prove our case. We don't know what documents we have to tender. As Your Honour is appreciative, until this point, the Prosecution's documents have been in English and B/C/S. English, of course, being one of the working languages of the Tribunal. If the Prosecution does not know which documents it has to tender to prove its case, it does not know which documents it has the -- the Trial Chamber will not know which documents have to be translated into the other working language of the Tribunal, thus putting -- which means at the moment the Prosecution must tender all of them, thus presenting the Tribunal, that is the Tribunal as a whole, with great resource dilemmas. As it stands, the Prosecution must prove -- the Prosecution of course knows that it must prove its case and doesn't cavil in any way with that, but the Defence must take a sensible approach to stipulations and confining the issues at trial as to those which are not or should not be in issue in a case which is one purely of command responsibility. Other ramifications will be -- will be on the evidence which is called, the number of witnesses the Prosecution has to call, and the number it can call either under 89(F) or 92 bis. It just doesn't affect the Prosecution, it affects the Tribunal as a whole. It affects the Victims and Witnesses Unit; it affects the Trial Chamber's consideration of matters; it affects Your Honour's determination today as to which witnesses the Prosecution can call, which crime base witnesses we can call, in what order, and how long we can call them for. If we can't get any agreement on the most basic of details, such as the deaths of people and even the manner of death, we will have to start right at the beginning and go through the whole thing, one after the other. It's a determination, in my submission, Your Honour will have a great difficulty in making today without knowing what the issues are before Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Prosecutor. Thank you. So it emanates from the comments by the Prosecution that regarding the points of agreement or disagreement on facts and points of law, the Prosecution is currently in a position when it doesn't have from the Defence, with the exception of a few cases, any specification, and as a result of that, the Prosecution is having difficulties concerning the calling of witnesses, the order of witnesses and, therefore, the conduct of the trial as such regarding the evidence to be called by the Prosecution. Therefore, the Prosecution is conveying a serious problem that it has. Of course, the Chamber needs to hear the Defence on these points, too. And the Defence, if it wishes, may agree with the Prosecution, but it may also not agree on any of those points. And it is up to the Defence to take a position in accordance with its own interests. And if the Defence does not agree in any respect with the Prosecution, it is up to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Prosecution to call the witnesses that it wishes to call. I shall now give the floor to Defence counsel for Mr. Hadzihasanovic first.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we looked at the problem in the sense it has been posed by the Prosecution, but we had just two days to do that. At the previous Status Conference, we discussed the facts, and one particular fact that we had received 165 pages just one day in advance, with about 1.200 points which the Prosecution offers to discuss and to try and find an agreement on. Now, bearing in mind first and foremost the rights of our client to a fair trial and an expeditious trial, we have invested maximum efforts to ensure that we have deliberated the document in detail, and we have done our best to help reach an agreement and send in to the Prosecution everything that the Defence counsel has to say with respect to the facts, and we have done this in good faith. You drew our attention to that at the previous Status Conference. After a detailed examination of the matter in hand, we said that as this is a vast document indeed, compiled in such a way which has not been customary thus far before this Tribunal, and for the most part following future solutions in which the Prosecution offers us all the facts which he intends to prove, we nonetheless approach this problem by carefully looking at all the facts set out. And we said that we should do our best to comply with the 15-day deadline. However, the task was far greater than you could have expected us to get through realistically, and I think you, Your Honour, said words to that effect at the previous Status Conference, and I think you were fully conscious of that task. Both Defence teams worked on issues that they could confirm jointly, and we informed the Prosecution on time, within the deadline, that all the facts we agree with we will supply in a short space of time. But we also emphasise that this was a hefty process of coordination and agreement and that we should continue to work along those lines. And in that sense, by a joint Defence brief, we agreed to 29 points set forth, and at the same time emphasised that we would continue our discussions about the possible acceptance by the 26th of November of the others, because as you know, none of the members of the Defence team actually lives in The Hague, which means we cannot plan our time for discussions the way in which the Prosecution can and the OTP, who is here permanently. Unfortunately, after this lengthy work done by us and our readiness to continue to negotiate and discuss additional points, we were faced with a letter which had already been addressed to you in which the Defence is placed in the position of being responsible for not having coordinated and dovetailed additional facts. I have had quite a long time of experience working in the law, and I consider that discussions between the Defence teams and the Prosecution must always be in good faith and done in a professional manner. The way in which the Prosecution on this occasion has conducted itself towards the Defence seemed to us to be an invitation that this professional relationship be translated into something else, something which we do not wish to see, and that is a conflict between us with respect to issues we have to work on together if this trial is to be a fair one, and that is why we reject methods of this kind. At this point in time, we have provided the Prosecution with everything that we were able to agree on fully by the deadline. We're still working along those lines to look through and study all the facts presented to us and disclosed to us by the Prosecution, and we consider that it is up to the Trial Chamber to assist and support this process of further harmonisation and coordination. I should just like to ask my colleague Mr. Stephane Bourgon to present some concrete facts to clarify the position that the Defence finds itself and has been finding itself over the past month. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Residovic. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following the statement by my colleague in response to the arguments presented by the Prosecution, I should just like to underline a few measures that we took with a view to facilitating the process of stipulation with our colleagues from the Prosecution. First of all, the Prosecution tells you that we have received their documents, that is the pre-trial brief, within a shorter time limit so as to enable us to come to an agreement regarding certain admissions of fact. This document was given to us, and we have studied that document, and we were already then ready to engage in discussions regarding possible admissions of fact. Shortly after that, the Prosecution notified us of their intention to serve documents on us which would contain proposals for stipulations, and we agreed with that, and we informed the Prosecution that we would wait for that document before going forward with the stipulation process. This document was served on us on the 4th of November, which means after the filing of the pre-trial brief on the 10th of October and after the filing of the Defence pre-trial brief on the 3rd of November. On the 4th of November, we were, therefore, seized of this document which contains 1.200 proposed stipulations. Since the beginning of this pre-trial procedure, we have communicated with the Prosecution. We have conveyed to them our intention, as far as possible, to make stipulations so as to allow the proceedings to be rather short but which would at the same time be a fair one and which would respect the rights of the accused. This position on the part of the Defence has not changed today. We are still of the opinion that we are ready to contribute to this process, and we are interested in making stipulations so as to allow the Chamber to make progress more rapidly with the proceedings. Nonetheless, within this context we also provided the Prosecution with a document, a document entitled "Stipulations Proposed by the Defence." In that document, as noted by the Prosecutor, we find facts which were already the object of judgements in other cases, that is in the Blaskic case, in the Kordic case, but also in other cases which are not under appeal, such as Kupreskic, Furundzija, and other cases. The aim of the Defence in giving this document to the Prosecution was also in a spirit of cooperation to allow the Prosecution to also make certain stipulations to alleviate our burden but also to alleviate the cross-examination of its own witnesses. If the Prosecution were to make certain admissions regarding the facts that we proposed, in our opinion this could considerably reduce the questions that would be put in the cross-examination of these witnesses. The Prosecution tells us in a document that was mentioned by my learned colleague that the Defence -- that the Prosecution believes that the Defence is going to apply a reprisal defence or a defence based on the tu quoque principle. First of all, Mr. President, it should be noted that the Prosecution has no reason whatsoever to try and qualify or to mention to the Chamber what will be, according to it, the defence that we will make in the course of the trial. However, even if the Defence wished to apply the principle of reprisal or tu quoque principle, we are not in a stage where we are going to argue on the admissibility of a certain kind of defence. However, it should be noted that the Prosecution said today that our arguments are not relevant, that the admissions that we're asking from the Prosecution are not relevant and that those stipulations apparently have nothing to do with the case that we are concerned with. And our response to that, Mr. President, is either that the Prosecution has not understood at all the doctrine of command responsibility or it doesn't wish to. But we are not declaring either of these options to be the one we're asserting. It could be a third one. However, we do assert that in our opinion, the stipulations that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. we proposed to the Prosecution are facts within the context and within the situation in which the accused were put, that is as military commanders in an armed conflict, a highly complicated armed conflict, about which you will obtain all the details during the presentation of the evidence. And when it comes to judging the responsibility of the commanders to see, first of all, whether, yes or no, he was responsible for certain troops, then the context is very important. When it comes to the question of demonstrating to this Chamber whether the accused knew or had reason to know what was happening among the troops under his control, then the context is of primordial importance. When it comes to showing to the Chamber whether the accused took measures which were necessary and reasonable to remedy the situation or to prevent the commission of crimes, the context is again, in our opinion, of prime importance. In view of that, we take note of the refusal of the Prosecution to make stipulations in accordance with our suggestions, and consequently we're going to present to this Chamber a motion that the Chamber take judicial notice of these facts which have already been proven and adjudicated in other trials, other cases. Obviously, we would prefer to engage in this same process but in a friendly manner, in a professional manner, in discussions with the Prosecution to come to an agreement on certain facts, to avoid us having to submit, to address yourselves to you, Mr. President, regarding admission of facts that have already been proven in trials conducted by the Office of the Prosecutor, which is unique and which stands for all the Prosecutions. So when we hear the Prosecution say that we are acting in bad faith, that we are not serious, that we do not wish to make any stipulations, I think that is not a good way of describing the discussions we had before you, of describing them to you. To link up with the stipulations that are required of us by the Prosecution, I could perhaps, Mr. President, suggest that you look at the three points mentioned by the Prosecutor today. The Prosecutor mentioned A.17, A.18, and A.19. These are points of fact which the Prosecutor considers to be part of the law. If the Prosecutor believes that these are points -- part of the law, why do we need to stipulate on them? If those points are so evident, so obvious, why are we asked to make stipulations on these points? The question, Mr. President, is we feel that these three points, which are not part of the admissions that we made in a document of the 24th of November are points which are, in our opinion, it is not possible on the 24th of November to make an admission, a stipulation. And to tell you today, Mr. President, we agree with these three points. These three points have an incidence, an effect, we believe, on the responsibility of the commander. And we also believe they have an effect on the relationship that could have existed between the two accused in this case. Before being able to pronounce ourselves on these points, in our opinion, we need to be able to discuss these matters first with the representatives of the co-accused in this case, to then take a position which would be common and in the interest of the accused and then to meet with the Prosecutor to discuss these points with them face-to-face. I refer to the letter of the 24th of November, which was sent to you in an annex with the opinion of the Prosecutor last Tuesday. In this letter, we made several admissions, and we indicated our wish to continue the process, and we also indicated that certain admissions or stipulations simply required an adjustment in terms of words. It is easy to launch a document of 1.200 facts and to expect a yes or no answer. We believe that in a face-to-face meeting between professionals, we could indicate to the Prosecutor that we are ready to stipulate on an additional point, but perhaps two or three words need to be changed. But one cannot do that without having a really professional meeting. And on this point, Mr. President, you will be able to note that in the admissions filed or proposed by the Prosecution, as was correctly stated by the Prosecutor, there's line-by-line the evidence that they intend to produce, the burden of proof, line by line according to the indictment. Since we are on this subject and this is not something that we need to discuss before you, we feel, but the 1.200 facts proposed to us are often taken from documents that will be presented before this Chamber. And we believe that the text that was added within these 1.200 proposals by the Prosecution does not always reflect, at least not always, the verbatim text of those documents. So you can imagine, Mr. President, that when one compares a document that we have, and we know that it will be produced in evidence, and then we have a stipulation and then there's a difference between the words used in the two. So to be able to make the bridge between the document and the proposal of the Prosecution, we need to meet to discuss it, which is what we intended to do on Wednesday, that is two days ago, and we appeared with the intention to have a discussion, and I think this is referred to in our response. We filed a response to the opinion of the Prosecution in which we said that we were ready to discuss the following facts: A4, C1, C3, C25, D3, D4, D5, D6, D7, G6, G7, G8, G61, G71, G72, G73, G75, G77 and G79. It is not possible to tell you today that we would have come to an agreement on each of those points, but we were ready to discuss them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please slow down because of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were ready to discuss these things. And I'm not in a position to tell you today whether we would have come to an agreement but we were in good faith, and I have the text before me here that I could maybe even present to the Judge, that is the text that we thought we could propose to the Prosecution with a view to accelerating the proceedings. Two conclusions, Mr. President: The first regarding the matter of resources. The Prosecutor refers to a theme throughout its request, that is in its opinion of last Tuesday and the motion filed this morning, a repetitive theme regarding the resources of the Tribunal. Mr. President, if there is someone in this hall, people in this hall who are fully aware and who have even suffered because of certain restraints during the last 12 months, then they are representatives of the Defence. I will not go into the detail, because they have already been the object of debate, however, I can tell you that this question was a heavy burden for the Defence, and it prevented us on many occasions from going forward more quickly. Nonetheless, the proceedings begin today. We are now at the Pre-Trial Conference, and the trial itself will begin on Tuesday. We would like, and we wish to express our wish today that the trial evolve as quickly as possible and that we can focus truly on the questions in dispute. In order to be able to do that, we believe, Mr. President, that the Prosecution is able to indicate today the witnesses it will call in evidence. Where there is a problem - and we would like there not to be any problems, but where -- if there is a problem is if the Prosecution wants to call a witness and the Defence stands up and tells you, "The Defence has no questions," at that point one could say there we have a problem, because then we have asked a witness to come from ex-Yugoslavia, to appear here before you, to spend days in The Hague spending resources, whereas in fact the Defence has no questions for him. Then we would be liable to criticism, criticism which we would accept, but we submit that that will not happen. When on the 13th of November the Prosecutor asked us what are we going to do with our witnesses from Dusina, what are we going to do with our witnesses, should we call them? We are facing a difficult situation. In our opinion, this was already the beginning of animosity, but we responded immediately, saying the witnesses that you have envisaged for Dusina, you can call them because we do need to cross-examine them. In this connection, the Prosecutor knows which are the witnesses they will begin with, because they've already told us that they will begin with Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Dusina, so we don't see any cause for alarm or we do not see any crisis that the Prosecutor is attempting to convey to you this morning. They know which witnesses they can call, and we are going to continue to participate in this debate openly, professionally, and to make stipulations. But if the Prosecutor asks us today do we have other stipulations to make, for the moment - and I speak for the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic - we have no other stipulations to make today. For today, we have communicated the stipulations that we are ready to make. We have a series of stipulations that I've referred to and that we are ready to discuss with the Prosecution which could facilitate the proceedings at the beginning but which will have no impact on the witnesses that need to be called or the documents that will be tendered. And professionally, we hope that we will be able to continue this debate and this discussion with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I shall now give the floor to the Defence counsel for Mr. Kubura regarding the same question. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, briefly, and with the greatest respect to my learned friends from the Prosecution, I think much too much is being made of this matter. I cannot underline enough that the admissions that have been made are only a first stage, and if I can at this point clarify that the admissions that have been made have been made on behalf of Mr. Hadzihasanovic and Mr. Kubura. There are joint admissions, they are 30 altogether, and that was conveyed to the Prosecution, that they are admissions made on behalf of both of the defendants. But they are a first stage in the proceedings, as was outlined in previous Rule 65 ter meetings with your Senior Legal Officer. And even as Mr. Withopf said in the last Status Conference, if we could get from the Defence admissions on a rolling basis, so according to how the Prosecution is going to present their case, and we can take it step-by-step. It's a mammoth task, simply put, Your Honour, to try and now at the beginning of the trial agree or not agree on all of the facts in the case. And that is the way we've approached the matter for Mr. Kubura. We obviously, as Your Honour knows, did not have to look at the matter of Dusina as he's not charged with that, but we have looked at the general matters that pertain to him relevant to the beginning of the case, and we've looked at Miletici, which he is charged with, and we have at this stage made the admissions that we can make. We are now going to be going on to Maline and to the others after that and we will then make further stipulations to the Prosecution, and I think this is a process that the Prosecution should have been aware of. This is not an end of the matter as far as we're concerned. Your Honour, we would therefore request you to allow the parties to continue on this process of seeing what stipulations can be made, and where no agreement can be reached, then it's for obvious reasons, and it is then for the Prosecution to present their case. We do find it difficult to understand how if the Defence hasn't made admissions the Prosecution doesn't know what evidence they have to lead. It's precisely because we are not agreeing to facts that we are saying you must prove those matters, and it's then for the Prosecution to present their case. Finally, Your Honour, in respect of the stipulations which the Defence has put forward for the Prosecution to admit or not, our basic point is if the Prosecution can tell us as soon as possible whether they do admit those points or not. In our submission, at this stage it's not relevant to discuss what are the inferences that can be drawn from those facts, how they can be used. That's a matter for trial. At this point all we wish to know is whether those facts are admitted or not, because if not, then other actions are going to have to be taken. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Regarding the question raised by the motion, the Chamber notes today that the Prosecution is expressing fears regarding the continuation of the proceedings because the Prosecution, they say, is not able to have a precise understanding of the witnesses it should call and the facts or points of law which, due to a specific response from the Defence, they say, still remain ambiguous. The Defence unanimously tells us that today there is some 30 points which are not in dispute and which could be admitted out of the 1.200 points that were proposed by the Prosecution. The Defence wishes to continue this process of discussion with the Prosecution with a view to avoiding, as they say, the expenditure of Tribunal resources inappropriately to the extent that witnesses cited by the Prosecution may not be cross-examined, and that is why the Defence requests that the Prosecution amends certain terms in the 1.200 points so that they can come to an agreement. So that would summarise the position of the Defence. On the other hand, the Defence for Mr. Hadzihasanovic has notified the Chamber that it has submitted to the Prosecution also a certain number of facts which require no comment from the Prosecution, whereas the Prosecution says that these facts are not related to the trial that is beginning on Tuesday, though the Defence indicates that these facts are relevant for the context. Therefore, the Chamber is going to render, following the motion, a written order, and I would like to indicate the substance of it. The Chamber is going to invite the Defence and the Prosecution, by Monday at 5.00 p.m., to meet in order to find possible new points of agreement and to indicate in a document addressed to the Chamber on Monday at 5.00 p.m. the final position of the Defence regarding the 1.200 points proposed by the Prosecution. Therefore, you will have this afternoon and all of Monday, until 5.00 p.m., to find a solution. If no solution is found, the trial will begin on Tuesday as envisaged, but then, of course, it will be up to the Prosecution, as excellently indicated by the Defence, to prove through its witnesses the facts alleged in the indictment. Therefore, that would be the ruling of the Chamber regarding this point. And you will have this order very shortly. We will now move on to the next point. However, in view of the time, we are going to have a brief adjournment to allow the interpreters to rest unless the Prosecution wishes to intervene once again on this point. Yes, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution will keep its observations very short. We heard the lengthy interpretation by the Defence teams, in particular by the Hadzihasanovic Defence team on this issue. The interpretation is one side, the facts are the other side, and the facts in this case speak for themselves. What are the 1.200 proposed admissions? The 1.200 proposed admissions are nothing else but details that are contained in the indictment, details that the Defence knows since more than two years. They are, in addition, details from witness statements, witness statements which have been disclosed to the Defence on an ongoing basis, many of them many months ago, and they are details of documents which have been disclosed to the Defence at the very early stages of the proceedings. I am referring to the so-called Sarajevo collection. This has been made available to the Defence at the very, very early stages of the proceedings. The Prosecution is very appreciative for the suggestion you have made, Your Honour, to meet and to continue to discuss any potential stipulations. The Prosecution was always inviting Defence, on a permanent and repeated basis, to meet and to discuss stipulations. Defence indicated in respect to their proposed admissions that they may or may not file a motion for judicial notice, inviting the Trial Chamber to take judicial notice. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. The Prosecution, I can already announce it now, will respond to this motion seeking dismissal of the motion. The Prosecution is of the view that the facts as proposed by the Defence are neither common knowledge nor are they adjudicated facts. They are not adjudicated facts because the vast majority of such facts are still under appeal. In respect to the translation of documents, one of the main points Defence for the accused Hadzihasanovic was trying to make, I again emphasise such documents have been made available to the Defence since months. It is the first time today the Defence raises any translation issues. And I also wish to emphasise that most -- the vast majority of the details in the document on proposed admissions, the vast majority are details that stem from witness statements, witness statements very well known to the Defence since many years. The Prosecution understands that Defence may in respect to the one or the other proposed fact may not be in a position, may not be in a position to say yes or no. For that purpose, Your Honours, the Prosecution has provided to the Defence the document on proposed admissions in an electronic version in order to allow, to allow the Defence to change and to alter such admissions and to come back to the Prosecution. Defence didn't do. Because of the unwillingness and unpreparedness of Defence to do, to finally do what they announced since many months, we are left with the current situation which creates huge difficulties not only for the Prosecution as outlined by my colleague Mr. Re, but also for the Trial Chamber, and such difficulties we are facing at the very beginning of the trial. The Prosecution again invites, based on the announced order by Your Honour, invites Defence to meet Prosecution and to now come to a conclusion what their position will be, and of course by 5.00 the latest on Monday such a filing will be filed. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. So the Chamber has taken note of what the Prosecution has just said. We are now going to adjourn for 15 minutes, and we will resume at ten to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now examine the question of the number of witnesses that the Prosecution intends to call. Having said that the Prosecution has already provided the Defence with a list of witnesses, and in that list we have 134 -- we had 134 witnesses, and at the last Status Conference the Prosecution told us that they had ten or so more witnesses, and in view of the fact that there was no agreement reached on facts, is the Prosecution in a position to tell us the number of witnesses that they intend to call?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, you are very well aware of the difficult situation the Prosecution is in. As you mentioned, the Prosecution has currently 134 witnesses on its list. The Prosecution is forced to, at this point in time, work on the assumption that it has to call all witnesses as listed in its witness list attached to the pre-trial brief. In addition to the 134 listed on our list, we will, as repeatedly announced, call an expert witness -- a military expert witness, namely General Rheinhardt. In respect to the witness list, two out of the 134 witnesses unfortunately have died, one of them only recently. These are the ones as listed in the witness list as annexed to the Prosecution's pre-trial brief under numbers 5 and 13. In respect to such witnesses, we will file respective motions under Rule 92 bis (C) in the near future. That means there are still 132 witnesses on the Prosecution's witness list and the military expert. Only recently -- addressing the issue of potential additional witnesses, only recently, two weeks ago, the Prosecution interviewed, or started to interview a number of additional potential witnesses; more concrete, about eight of such individuals. Not all of such individuals will be added to the witness list, maybe the one or the other. That means that we are at this point in time, we are talking about some 135 witnesses on the Prosecution's witness list. To date we have received 25 declarations under Rule 92 bis (B). We anticipate, as we already announced in the course of the last Status Conference, to get some ten to 15 more within the first few weeks after the commencement of the trial. Summarised, the Prosecution intends to call, based on the current situation we are in, intends to call about 95 to 100 witnesses live. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Therefore, as of this day you intend to call 100 viva voce witnesses and about 40 other witnesses pursuant to Rule 92 bis. And with respect to 89(F) witnesses, you're not going to avail yourself of that possibility. Now, with respect to the number of witnesses that you gave, two are deceased, and without any objection from the Defence, we hope perhaps you're going to have written testimony by these witnesses tendered. So it is 5 and 13 of those. That's what you told us. So at this stage, with respect to the fact that you said you would be bringing about 100 witnesses, would the Defence like to make any observations on that score?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I answer your question, I would like to tell you that both Defence teams discussed the issues raised by you on the agenda today and with full respect for your time and joint stands with respect to individual issues, we shall be presenting the joint views of the two Defence teams, and I myself will be presenting our views for the Hadzihasanovic Defence team and Brigadier Kubura as well. The OTP disclosed to us on time lists of witnesses. We have nothing to add with respect to that matter except to say that we have heard today that the Prosecution will probably be adding to that list a number of other witnesses. As we have heard, he is negotiating this possibility with eight individuals. It is our common stand that finally, after more than two years since the first initial appearance of the accused before the Tribunal, the Prosecution should provide us with the final list of witnesses he intends to call. With respect to Rule 92 bis, we have just heard from the Prosecutor that he wishes to use 425 -- this 425 witnesses and we have already told the Prosecution that we should like to ask him to tender a request so that in conformity with Rule 92 bis (A) to (F) [as interpreted], he provide reasons, stipulate the reasons for which he considers those statements should be accepted, because then we have the possibility within a space of a seven-day time limit to respond to the proposal made by the Prosecution. For the purposes of better understanding the positions taken by the Defence, although I don't think this has been challenged, all we wish to say is this, that the statements of these witnesses in fact, as interpreted by the Defence, are just facts which testify to the fact that the witness would repeat what he has set out in his written statement if he were called to testify orally. However, the weight and truthfulness of that testimony and its credibility will be weighed up together with all the other evidence, and that is of course the -- what the Trial Chamber has to do. So the Defence considers that these are not adjudicated facts, but we do accept that the statements which are presented before the Court are statements by those individuals which they would have given if they were here physically and presented their testimony orally. So that is our position respect to the two issues raised by the Prosecutor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to Rule 92 bis witnesses, the Chamber is fixing the 18th of December as the limit for the response by the Prosecution, and the Defence is also invited to make its observations by the 12th of January, because as you know, we're going to have a pause of several weeks. There will be a recess at the end of December until the beginning of January, court recess, and so the Prosecution has the deadline of the 18th of December, whereas the Defence has been given the 12th of January as a deadline pursuant to Rule 92 bis (B) witnesses. With respect to witnesses, the Chamber would like to suggest at this stage that either the Prosecution or the Defence possibly, or perhaps the Chamber itself, pursuant to Article 89, that it brings in an expert in history in order to place matters in the political and historical context of the events and the acts committed. I haven't seen any name put forward, but if the Prosecution hasn't thought about it, perhaps the Defence could give thought to it. If neither side do, then the Trial Chamber can call such a witness itself, after we have heard debate and discussion, and then we would call a witness of that kind pursuant to the Rule allowing the Chamber to call witnesses. So that is a proposal on my part to both parties, to the Prosecution and the Defence. Now, unless there is anything -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I just inform you that we have already taken steps and asked the Registrar and received confirmation for us to bring in an expert witness who would be speaking of the historical context within the Defence case, and that would be one expert on the part of the Defence brought in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution has the floor on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The Prosecution suggests that the Chamber calls, pursuant to Rule 98, an expert of such nature proprio motu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, I'd like to go on to the next point, which is the protective measures which may be sought in respect of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, to emphasise it, from the outset in this trial protective measures for Prosecution witnesses are, in comparison to many other cases, likely not to be a major issue. Out of the 132 witnesses currently on the list, 15, only 15 for the time being have assigned pseudonyms. I refer to the numbers 3, 35, 55, 72, 78, 81, 86, 96, 100, 103, 104, 106, 108, 107, and 130 on the confidential witness list. We would not even be surprised if at the end of the day there may be less such witnesses, even less for the following reason: We made the experience that once the trial team lawyers talked to the witnesses and explained to them the situation in respect to Rule 75 and any protective measures, such witnesses are quite often very confident and very prepared to drop their request for protective measures. If at all, there may be a few instances of assignment of pseudonyms and face and/or voice distortion. In such instances, we shall inform the Chamber in sufficient time in advance. There are a few insider-type of witnesses that may or may not request additional protective measures under Rule 75. The number of such witnesses will be limited, even presumably very limited. At this point we wish to point out that the Defence got all but one of our OTP witness statements; the military expert obviously will not request any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Now with respect to the protective measures, the Chamber has been informed of this in advance, and we would like to see the motions handed in to us one or two days before the witnesses arrive, because then we can put into place all the technical protective measures necessary in order to ensure protection for the witnesses. So I invite the Prosecution to let us know as early on as possible if they would like measures to be put in place of that kind. Now -- yes, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a practical -- it's a purely practical issue. Most of such witnesses would only arrive the day prior to their testimony, and the Prosecution trial team's lawyer will only have a chance to talk to the majority of such witnesses only the day prior to their testimony. We, of course, are very interested to give you the respective information as early as possible, but there may be instances that we can only provide you with the necessary information the day before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, yes. Thank you for that. But of course you can telephone them, perhaps, and certain witnesses do have mobile telephones. So you can come into contact with them by telephone perhaps. Having said that with respect to the order of witnesses, you have advised me of the planning for the next three weeks, from the 8th to the 10th of December, and the 15th to the 18th of December. So you have estimated the number of witnesses to be called during that time period. So we have a plan for our work already and with respect to hearings for those witnesses. Now, grosso modo, there will be one day per witness, roughly speaking. Would that be right? So we now have a project for the coming three weeks, and it would be advisable for the months to come that we could have a document of that kind, a plan which will allow us to plan for January, February, et cetera, and the coming months. Can the Prosecution enlighten us on that score with respect to proceeding in this way? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Right. Your Honour, as Defence already have the witness scheduled for the first three weeks of the trial prior to the winter recess, we are aiming at, to admit, December and provide you with a similar list for the month of January. As can be seen from our list, the Prosecution will commence trial with so-called crime base witnesses in relation to Dusina, in relation to Miletici, and Maline and Bikosi in exactly this order. There will be additional crime base witnesses in respect to the three crime scenes I just mentioned, to the three crime bases I just mentioned, and we anticipate that the Prosecution will have called all such witnesses by the day the Prosecution will call its military expert. The military expert will be called on Monday, the 26th of January, 2004. After the examination of the military expert, and we anticipate the Defence will cross-examine the military expert, and the military expert is informed that he has to make himself available for three days starting the 26th till the 28th of January, the Prosecution anticipates that it will continue with crime base witnesses following the order of the indictment. That would mean we will continue with the crime base witnesses related to the crimes in the detention facilities, then we would call in the witnesses in relation to the destruction and plunder crimes, and finally, we would call the witnesses in relation to the damage to the religious institutions. We are planning to, at the end of the trial, to call the so-called international witnesses, international witnesses as previous ECMM monitors, as UNPROFOR, predominantly BritBat members, and other internationals. Your Honour are certainly aware that quite a number of such witnesses are still serving soldiers, serving soldiers in high ranks being dispersed all over the world, literally all over the world. We may face situations, and it's likely to happen, that we have to call the one or the other international witness in between different crime scene witnesses. However, we are aiming to have the witnesses being called for each section as much as possible, thus trying to avoid to jump from one crime base to the other one and trying to avoid that too many international witnesses have to be called in between the different crime scenes. That, in a nutshell, is the rough outline how we like to present the case, all based on the assumption that there will be no further stipulations by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We now have a plan of work presented to us by the Prosecution, and we're going to have witnesses that were sited where the places were given, at Dusina, Miletici, et cetera, and we're going to have an expert witness, a military one, and other witnesses who are going to be fact witnesses. And the Prosecution has proposed to call, finally, international observers as witnesses. So we have a plan which is fairly precise and detailed for the weeks to come. Having said this, we come to another question, and that is the duration of the Prosecution evidence pursuant to 73 (B) (C) (i) and (E) [as interpreted] on the basis of a calculation for testimony on the basis of one day per witness, roughly. If we look at the number of witnesses we're going to have, 100 plus 40, pursuant Article 92 bis, having received that information, the Chamber can now fix in conformity with that and with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence a total duration of Prosecution evidence pursuant to 73 bis, Rule 73 bis, to fix here and now a maximum deadline on the 1st of June, 2004. That would be the date for the duration of the Prosecution case. As you know, if additional time proves to be necessary pursuant to Rule 73 bis (E), then the Prosecution can send in a motion asking for more time, and the duration of time provided for has to take into consideration the presentation of the case itself plus six months, and that would be the time accorded. But I would like to set the date as being the 1st of June, 2004 for the Prosecution case. If the Prosecution feels it necessary to extend that time, that is, of course, possible. So would anybody like to make any observations with respect to the date I have just quoted? Yes, the Prosecution has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution is fine with the date you've just mentioned. It actually matches exactly the duration of the presentation of the Prosecution's case the Prosecution has announced once they filed their pre-trial brief. Of course the presentation of the Prosecution case depends on the duration of the cross-examination of the Prosecution witnesses by the Defence. Your Honour made already a reference to the respective provision under Rule 73 bis (E), if necessary, I repeat, if necessary, the Prosecution would make use of this provision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence. Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course the length of the duration of the trial and the presentation of the Prosecution case is something that the Prosecution has already set out, and you have made a ruling on that as the Trial Chamber. The Defence presented some of its views, but the Defence does not wish in any way to make any criticisms or comments with respect to a ruling which has been reached between the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution presenting the case. However, as far as the Defence is concerned, there's one question that remains unsolved, and that, with the adoption of the new method of payment for the Defence team, has remained unsettled. This is what it is about: Rule 98 bis determines the right accorded to the Defence that after the Prosecution case has gone forward, it can make proposals to make an acquittal decision on some or all counts in the indictment. The new Rules state that this right, motion for judgement of acquittal, could be used by the Defence case in the course of the presentation of the Prosecution case. And we should now like to ask you, Your Honour, to tell us whether this means that by the 1st of July, one month or two months will be set - this has been the practice - and given to the Defence to present its final document after it has heard the Prosecution case, or is the date that you gave us the time when the Prosecution finishes its Prosecution case? So as there's a slight discrepancy between what Rule 98 bis states and the new way in which the lump sum and payment of attorneys is established, we should like to ask the Trial Chamber to consider this matter and to give us its decision and ruling pursuant to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your question has two aspects, in fact. There is the question linked to the implementation of Rule 98 bis regarding the date by which the motion for acquittal may be filed and the question of remuneration. So I will answer also in two sections. The first: Rule 98 bis is very precise. It says that an accused may file a motion for the entry of a judgement of acquittal on one or more offences charged in the indictment within seven days after the close of the Prosecution's case. So if the end of the Prosecution case will be the 1st of June, you will have seven days after the 1st of June, except if the Prosecution files a motion to extend the time, then the time will run from the date that will be fixed in response to a motion from the Prosecution. Therefore, regarding the first aspect, there are no problems. It is very precise. As soon as the Prosecution evidence has been presented, and it will be noted that there will be no more evidence or witnesses for the Prosecution, from that point on the time will begin to run, that is, the seven days within which you may file a motion for a judgement of acquittal. That is the first point. The second: You're linking the question of remuneration of Defence attorneys with this date. Regarding this question, as you know, the remuneration is within the terms of reference of the Registry. Therefore, it is to them that you should address yourself. And the Chamber has no competence with respect to questions of remuneration. Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could I please elaborate on what I said, namely, it is quite clear that Rule 98 bis gives us a time limit of seven days. Then the Prosecution has time to respond, then comes oral argument, and a final ruling of the Court. This may last one month, more or less, depending on the motion itself and the pleadings of the two sides, but the time limits are fixed by the Rules of this Tribunal. However, the most recent decision, which includes a schedule of payment for attorneys, in point C10 says that the Trial Chamber will, within the Prosecution period, include the time that is necessary for work to be completed linked to 98 bis. That was why I asked whether the Prosecution period is extended for a period that the Trial Chamber will fix for completing the whole procedure under Rule 98 bis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this clarification, but the question you are raising will come into consideration if there is an extension of time. Then the Defence will always have time to inform us or to raise the matter then. We cannot address a question that may arise within that period. So depending on the plan of work, the number of witnesses, we will see. Sometime in May, beginning of May, we can reconsider this question. So we'll leave that question on standby while we see how the trial itself proceeds. The other question has to do -- I'm sorry. Mr. Bourgon, you wish to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, with your permission, Your Honour, I should like to make one last remark on this subject. And I quite agree with you that it is disagreeable or that -- to talk about the remuneration of attorneys during the trial, and it would be best if we could not mix the two, but regarding the point we would like to draw attention to is that the date that you are fixing today is a date which has a direct impact on the amount of the fees given to the attorneys as of next week, because according to the directive that's required -- that the date that is required by this directive must cover the period until the ruling under 98 bis. So the magic figure that will be part of the calculation of remuneration is six months. And for the Registry, they will take into consideration that after six months the Chamber has ruled on 98 bis. If you tell us today that we are going to have this stipulated period after the Prosecution case, it means the Prosecution case ends on the 1st of June, seven days later we file our motion, 14 days later the Prosecution responds, and then after that the Chamber renders its decision, which on the basis our discussions with the senior trial attorney, could last about two months. So this magic figure, if I can use this word, will not be six but eight months, and for the Defence, this is a figure that has a very great importance in view of the fact that this figure will be part of the calculation for the remuneration of attorneys. And I do apologise for having to address this mention -- this issue during the Pre-Trial Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this point which is important for the Defence, you will always have an opportunity to file a motion, and of course the Chamber will consult the Registrar, and you will have a decision on this particular aspect. But for the moment, in view of the planning made by the Prosecution, we can estimate that by 1st of June, 2004, the Prosecution case will be completed except if there are exceptional circumstances that may arise in the meantime. But of course you can address us with a motion to raise this issue and a decision will be rendered in writing. Concerning the exhibits. As you know, the Prosecution has provided a list of 983 exhibits. To be admitted, these exhibits, naturally, have to be translated either into English or into French. It would be desirable, in view of the composition of the Chamber, that to the extent possible, the exhibits or documents be translated into French. Therefore, if we have a document which is in B/C/S, then of course it has to be translated into English and French. If it is in English, it needs to be translated for the Defence in the B/C/S because the accused must be able to read it, and into French. So I can imagine that there may be a problem of translation and, therefore, I'm asking the Prosecution regarding this question of translation of exhibits whether the list of 983 documents is final or will there be an additional list; and if so, will there be -- or will there be exhibits that will be removed from the original list? And the Defence, which of course is familiar with this list, is it able today to indicate whether there are exhibits that it will challenge the authenticity of. So these are a number of questions that I would like to hear the parties respond to. The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, most of the documents that do form part of our exhibit list have been translated. They have been translated either into English if they were B/C/S documents, or into B/C/S if they were English documents. There are a few ones left. We are receiving translations each and every day, and such translation are disclosed to the Defence on an ongoing basis. The current list, the current list of documents will not be the final list. There may be additional documents. On the list, what we, however, wish to emphasise is that Defence got all the documents and including the ones which may be added to the exhibit list. Of course, it also again, and I regret that I have to emphasise it again, it depends on the stipulations of the Defence. Translations into French, Your Honour, this is a very difficult and a very serious problem for us. There are none of such documents translated into French yet. We were working on the basis of the message that had been conveyed in one of the 65 ter meetings, that Chambers would take care of translation into French of what they consider being the core or the crucial documents. Taking into account the limited resources of the Prosecution, it will unfortunately not be possible that the Prosecution can take care of translations into French. I am, of course, not in a position to talk about CLSS and whether they can make the resources available at this short notice that would be required in this case. To summarise it, translations are mostly done. Defence got the relevant documents. Translation into French is a problem the Prosecution cannot solve. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Regarding translations, has the Defence any observations to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Before addressing the question of translation, I think it is important first of all to understand one another regarding the documents that need to be disclosed by the Prosecution to the Defence. The list in question, the Prosecutor tells us today that we have received all the documents which the Prosecution intends to use. We are of the opposite opinion, and we can verify this. I mentioned during the Status Conference several weeks ago that certain documents were missing, and I am able to inform the Chamber today according to our investigation of the documents that were disclosed to us. First of all, there are documents which are cited in the pre-trial brief and which are -- which carry the letters PT. And among those documents there are 43 that we cannot find on the list of documents. An example, there's a reference to a document PT44. We look at the list and there is no PT44. So we don't know what document that is. And there are 43 such documents. The second type of document are documents bearing the letters PTW, which are cited in the Prosecution pre-trial brief and which again are not to be found on the list of documents given to us. We are talking here about 113 documents. An example: Document 628 PTW, cited in the pre-trial brief, cannot be found in the list of documents. Finally, Mr. President, there are documents which are on the list of documents given to us by the Prosecution. However, those documents, we never received copies of them either on paper or on a CD-ROM that were served by the Prosecution. And we're talking about 17 such documents. I have a document here which I'm ready to present before this Chamber and to give a copy to the Prosecutor. So before even we address the question of translation, we have to see whether the Prosecution has really fulfilled its obligation under Rule 65 ter to disclose to the Defence the list of all the documents that it intends to produce at trial, as well as copies of those documents that need to be provided to the Defence. And in both cases, I think that we have not fully -- that the Prosecution has not fully fulfilled its obligations in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I am going to give the floor to the Prosecution now, but the list produced by the Prosecution containing the documents, apparently the Defence absolutely necessarily has to have them. That is quite clear. And we're being told today that 43 documents of that type are missing. Also, the Defence is saying that on the Prosecution list, there are documents -- I'm sorry, brief, there is reference to certain documents - PT44 - that cannot be found anywhere. And this is a serious problem which we need to resolve as soon as possible, and to the extent to which the Defence is facilitating the work of the Prosecution, by providing a list with the missing documents on it. And according to the Defence list, all those documents are mentioned because we have document 44, 78, et cetera, and the Prosecution, I hope, is going to examine closely the mentioned documents, and could they already at this stage orally tell us what their position is regarding the fact that the Defence has not received the necessary documents. Yes, please, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course the Prosecution appreciates that the Defence has to get all documents at the very early stage and as soon as possible. Of course, I'm not in a position to discuss the one or the other document which has been specified by the Defence today. We recently got a letter from the Defence identifying a number of documents with PT numbers. These were mainly concerning translations. We provided a number of such documents to the Defence. In respect to the long list of PT numbers, we think, however, this has to be examined and will be examined immediately after this Pre-Trial Conference. We think that such documents are actually witness statements which are included in the CDs Defence counsel have got a few days after the filing of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. The Prosecution will certainly take care of all this issue and will solve the problem provided that there is a problem. My colleague will raise two further things.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just in relation to those, Your Honour, the -- if they are, as I suspect, witness statements, we gave them a PTW number. They would not have been included in the exhibit list because the witness statements would not be exhibits. The oral testimony of the witness would be -- would be the evidence before the Trial Chamber. In the pre-trial brief we referred to the evidence in the footnotes, PTW to refer the Defence to the witness statement of the person providing that evidence. That would not have been on the witness list as such. The second point is the Prosecution is in the process of filing a corrigendum based upon errors in the footnotes the Prosecution has found and the Defence has provided to us, particularly in relation to PTs and ERNs. As Your Honour might appreciate, there is a huge difficulty in using ERNs which are 16 figures -- 16 numerals long, so we used PT numbers to try and simplify it. Inevitably, some errors crept in. The corrigendum should be filed hopefully today or on Monday. We have to have it filed before trial so that everyone is completely clear as to the correct footnoting of the PTs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding this point, I am convinced that the Prosecution has taken note of the observation of the Defence and will very quickly address them, and there will be no further discussion on this point which can be resolved relatively easily and within a very short period of time. Regarding translations, has the Defence any problems relating to the translation of documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Regarding the question of translations, first of all, the translation of documents on the Prosecution list, as has just been indicated by my learned colleague from the Prosecution, we quite recently indicated the documents missing in translation, and they have been given to us in the meantime. So we see no major difficulty at this stage regarding the translation of documents that are on the Prosecution's list. Having said that, Mr. President, during the Status Conference, I made quite a lengthy speech, maybe too long, regarding the question of translation, and I would like to return to the question briefly by making a synthesis of the situation. We have received, for trial, resources for interpretation and translation. We have been authorised to use an interpreter to be able to communicate with the accused in the Detention Unit. So if I go to the Detention Unit, I can go there with an interpreter who will be remunerated by the Tribunal, so no difficulty on that score. However, there are no resources allotted to us during trial for the translation of documents. On the 12th of November, we sent a list of documents to the unit responsible for the Defence with a list of documents that need to be translated as a priority before the trial. This list consisted of documents which we intended to use in the cross-examination during the hearing of the Prosecution witnesses, and we specified that these were documents which addressed events in Dusina. Instructions were given to the Defence unit not to communicate the list or the documents to the translation service of the Tribunal and that those documents would not be translated. The consequences are of two kinds: First of all, it will not be possible for me, as Defence counsel who does not speak the Bosniak language, to prepare a cross-examination. Secondly, when using these documents, when the Defence is using them, either by my colleague who does speak the Bosnian language, the documents need to be translated by an interpreter viva voce, which risks considerable delays, in our opinion. I will give you a quick example: We have an important document of four pages which the Prosecution doesn't have. This document will be used in the cross-examination of a witness that will probably be appearing next week. This document is only in the Bosnian language for the moment. We don't have resources to have it translated, and we have been told we cannot address ourselves to the Tribunal translation services. Therefore, the cross-examination will be prepared by my colleague who speaks Bosnian, and she will do the cross-examination. This is a document of four pages which needs to be translated viva voce before the cross-examination begins. We feel that there may be a better way, a better solution which could save time during the hearings and which would also allow for the respect of the rights of the accused, that is for their Defence counsel to be able to work with documents. So we are suggesting, first of all, that we send the documents once again to the translation services of the Tribunal with a list of priorities, and to overcome the gap between the fact that the services cannot provide translations, that some minimal resources be provided for us to translate those documents. Therefore, if we cannot count on the services of a person to assist us in translating them urgently, then at least 75 hours per month would be sufficient to allow the two Defence counsels to cross-examine the witnesses but also to save time when those documents are used before the Trial Chamber. The problem of translation is much broader than the point I'm making today. We will make a motion to the Chamber informing them of other difficulties, but we feel that this is a simple and inexpensive method to overcome this difficulty.
