utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Yes. Regarding this question of documents produced by the Defence within the framework of the cross-examination, the Defence may produce documents which are not in the possession of the Prosecution to cross-examine the witness. Clearly those documents which are presented in the cross-examination must be understood by the Prosecution, and the Chamber will rule whether to admit them as an exhibit of the Defence and will decide which probative value to give to them. The best method, in my view, would be, as you know in advance the witnesses that will appear and according to your Defence strategy you know which documents you're going to produce, that the appropriate service of the Registry should be told of the urgency of those documents being translated. So if you're sending a four-page document, the question may arise whether the whole of those four pages need to be translated or only certain paragraphs. So then you can highlight them with a marker so that those passages be translated before the hearing. But in cases when, unfortunately for the Defence, this is not done, there is the risk of prolonging the hearing of the witness in cross-examination, there's always the possibility of translating viva voce those documents. The document may be placed under the ELMO, and then the interpreters will translate the said documents following instructions that you will give regarding this or that paragraph. But clearly it would be better for those documents to be translated in advance. So address your document to the appropriate service, and if there are difficulties on the day of the hearing of the witness, you will let us know from the beginning that the document could not be translated, that such-and-such a paragraph is relevant, and then everyone will devote attention to the matter. Regarding the suggestion of the Defence. Has the Prosecution any observation to make? Though this has to do with the Registrar and not the Prosecution, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You're completely right, Your Honour, it's a matter between Defence and Registry. The Prosecution can, however, also already foresee a number of problems, in particular if the Defence, as described by my learned colleague, will use documents which are in B/C/S and only certain portions are translated into English. The Prosecution in instances we may not yet foresee now may wish to read the full document which poses a bit of additional burden on the Defence and the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. I think that everybody will realise this inconvenience and work around it. Now, with respect to written documents and exhibits of the Prosecution. It would be advisable that those documents should be copied and seven copies provided; three for the Judges, one copy per Judge; one copy for the registrar -- legal officer; and one for the registrar; and if it is a Prosecution document, then two copies for the Defence. So this means seven copies in all of each particular document, whether they are Defence documents -- if they are Defence documents, we should like to ask them to provide the same number, even if those documents have not been translated. So it is up to you to photocopy the said documents. I'd now like to go on to the next point on our agenda, which is the current status of disclosure of exculpatory material pursuant to Rule 68 of the Rules. Now, at this stage, how do we stand with respect to exculpatory material? Has the Defence been informed by the Prosecution of the existence of documents pursuant to Rule 68 at all? May we hear from the Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, Rule 68 materials, exculpatory materials, have been disclosed on a very regular basis since the beginning of these proceedings. The ISU searches on the rule 68 materials are continuing and will continue in future. They have produced quite a number of search results which already have been disclosed to the Defence. Any further search results of materials that do fall within the scope of Rule 68 will be disclosed immediately. We again this week disclosed additional Rule 68 materials. We identified a number of search criteria for the Rule 68 searches. Out of about 250 such search criteria, more than 160 are done, including all the names of the witnesses which are detailed in the Prosecution witness list. Search priorities have been given to ISU to ensure that such areas that will be of relevance at whatever stage of the proceedings will be covered prior to them being dealt with in the course of this trial. The searches for the Hadzihasanovic and Kubura case are ISU search priority, and the search results will be available soon and the materials will be disclosed as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we hear the Defence on Rule 68, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can confirm that the Prosecution has indeed been supplying us with material pursuant to Rule 68 on a regular basis, but you know that after the 6th of November, the Prosecution disclosed pursuant to Rule 68 the Vitez collection with thousands of documents and, as my learned friend said, he also disclosed other documents pursuant to Rule 68 of which we have the findings of an expert witness with annexes used by the expert witness, and they too represent several thousand pages in bulk. And the Defence has undertaken to examine those documents, it is an ongoing process, but I think it is quite clear that in the short space of time we have available we cannot get through such a vast quantity of material. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for that, and that completes point 8, the current status of disclosure of exculpatory material pursuant to Rule 68 of the Rules. I should now like to go on to the next item on our agenda, that is to say procedure during the trial itself. As you know full well, based on the planning established, the trial opens on Tuesday at 9.00 in the morning. We -- it is provided for to have hearings every day from Monday to Friday, and it seems to me to be advisable to hold those proceedings that way -- in such a way that -- I know that the Defence counsel have to travel, and they would like to see the hearings begin on a Monday afternoon to accommodate for their travel plans, which means going on Monday afternoon, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, et cetera, depending on the availability of the courts, and to end the week on Friday by midday, Friday morning, and then to have plans for the following week, which means that we would have Friday afternoon free, the weekend, and Monday morning free. So I have addressed this and told this to the Registrar. I have conveyed your request with respect to general planning for -- and to have the courtroom available for the trial. So it would be advisable that, as I say, we have Friday afternoons and Monday mornings free, which would allow both parties to prepare themselves for the coming week. Since the hearings have already been programmed and planned up to the month of June, if any extraordinary instances arise and the two parties encounter difficulties on a particular day, a Monday, Thursday, Wednesday, or whatever day, would you please let us know well in advance for us to be able to cater to that difficulty and to cancel a hearing if there are valid reasons for that and to put it off to another day. Now with respect to the commencement of the trial, as you know pursuant to Article 84, we have preliminary declarations. Now, I'd like to ask the Prosecution whether it has envisaged how long its opening address will last.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, a rough estimate in respect to the opening statement, we anticipate it lasting for about one and a half hour, maybe one hour 15 minutes, maybe two hours, but it will be within one hour 15 to two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. I would like to address the Defence now. Does the Defence have any idea as to how long its opening statement will last following on from the Prosecution opening statement? Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have already informed the Prosecution, and we should now like to inform Your Honour that our opening statement will be made after we hear the presentation of the Prosecution case, in keeping with Rule 74 of the Rules of Evidence and Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Kubura Defence team will also avail itself of its right to present its opening statement prior to the Defence case itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we will have a Prosecution opening statement for two hours. Now, can we have any timing for the rest, for your opening statement, Ms. Residovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking at the translation here in the transcript. I'm not sure you understood me correctly. What I said was that the Defence will reserve its right to deliver its opening statement before the beginning of the Defence case and after the Prosecution case has been completed. So we're not going to present our opening statement before that, on the 2nd of December. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore I'm concluding that at this stage you don't know whether you're going to make an opening statement or not. You're waiting to hear the contents of the opening statement of the Prosecution and then decide whether to make one. Is that my understanding? No. Please clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Maybe I wasn't precise enough. The Defence will be making its opening statement before the beginning of the Defence case. Therefore, it is availing itself of its right to make that opening statement before the beginning of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Prosecutor, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: There is a different issue, Your Honour, we wish to address. It has nothing to do with the opening statement, but it has to do with the scheduling as it has been detailed by you, Your Honour. It is in respect to the Friday sessions. If we got it correctly, you were saying, Your Honour, that you, based on the wish of the Defence, wish to finish the Friday sessions by midday. We understand midday is about noon, about 12.00. That would mean that we would lose one hour, one and a half hours every Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, no. No. That the morning hearings go on from 9.00 until 2.15, as is customary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: That means including Friday as well, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Let me be more specific. Monday -- on Mondays, the hearings would begin at 2.15, that is Monday afternoon. Then Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday they will begin either at 9.00 or at 2.15, as there are trials that are going on in the courtroom - so this will depend on the availability of courtrooms - and on Fridays, we would begin at 9.00 and finish around 2.00, either quarter to two or 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That clarifies the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning the cross-examination. As you know, the examination of a witness by the Prosecution is going to take a certain amount of time, so the question arises as to the length of the cross-examination by the Defence. The Defence here consists of several members of the Defence teams and two accused. It would be desirable, to the extent possible, that the duration of the cross-examination by the two Defence teams should be equal to the duration of the examination-in-chief by the Prosecution. This could be observed if the Defence does not ask the same questions as the Prosecution. Regarding the duration of the cross-examination by the Defence, could the Defence at this stage already inform the Chamber of its wishes concerning duration? For the Defence of Hadzihasanovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, we should like to inform you that before the beginning of the cross-examination of each witness, the witness will inform you which of the accused will be the first to cross-examine in view of the fact that all witnesses' statements do not relate equally to both accused. Secondly, it is our submission that, as a rule, the cross-examination will not take longer than the examination-in-chief by the Prosecution, and I believe that we will be able to avoid repetition of the same questions, but I do appeal to you to have understanding - and I'm sure you do - that each Defence team has its own responsibility to bear and that it will address the questions that are of interest to their client. So only exceptionally will we ask the Trial Chamber to extend us extra time for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the Defence for Mr. Kubura on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have already informed our learned friends from the Prosecution that we will cross-examine witnesses separately if there is a possibility, and that is up to an agreement between the two Defence teams for a witness to be cross-examined jointly, we will inform both the Prosecution and the Chamber of that and in that way perhaps save some time for the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think that there will be no special difficulties regarding that point. Regarding the possibility of submission of motions, if a Chamber receives a motion, it would be desirable for the Defence to inform the legal officer of the Chamber of the matter that the motion relates to, if possible, before the beginning of the hearing. By informing the legal officer, it will be possible to establish whether the motion could be orally discussed or in written form, and if a motion relates to complex issues, then it would be better for it to be made in writing. That is for the possibility of having motions filed. To ensure the proper proceedings, try to inform the legal officer of the Chamber of such motions in advance, and then both the Prosecution and the Chamber would be informed about it in advance, and of course motions raising questions of substance should be put in writing. I hope there are no remarks regarding motions. I now pass on to another point which is still outstanding, and that is the question of the access of the Defence to the archives of the European Union. The Chamber has taken note of the Defence's communication with the Secretary-General on the 13th of November. At this stage, have you received any response? Because the procedure that you wish to set in motion by the European Union would consist of you going on site, examining the documents, indicating the relevant documents that you would wish to have, and then the European Union, resorting to Rule 70 or not, would communicate them to you. Could you address this point, please. Who wishes to take the floor?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, on behalf of the Defence, I can say that as of yet we have not got a response to that letter that Your Honour refers to. However, we have been informed that we will be getting a response soon, and we hope that we will have something in the next week with a response from them as to our proposal. The reason, Your Honour, why we put forward that proposal was so that we could go there and look at the documents, taking into account the concerns that the European Union has expressed, to see whether they're relevant for our case and then to seek permission for them to be used by us and potentially to be used in court. And we're hoping that that will be an acceptable method to the European Union. If it is and we get a response from them soon, then we will be taking the next step of going to examine the documents. Your Honour, there is another related matter, and that is that if we do not get a positive response from them, and indeed until the matter is resolved, until we get an answer from them, we would request that Your Honour orders that no witnesses from the European Union present evidence before the Trial Chamber so that we can look at the documents before those witnesses attend. And in addition, that no documents from the European Union are submitted as yet so that we could have an opportunity to look at the documents as a whole before any particular documents are used. So we would ask Your Honour's indulgence to rule that at this stage the European Union evidence is not relied upon by the Prosecution until this matter is resolved finally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Would the Prosecution like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, very briefly. This request by Defence appears to be very reasonable. We don't have any problem with it. I think it makes sense to wait another few weeks in order to get some sort of idea as to when Defence will be in a position to review the EMM documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. With respect to the Defence's access to confidential documents in other matters and in other cases, the Trial Chamber has seen that the documents with respect to the -- in the Kordic case was placed at your disposal. So I think that with respect to the procedure that you have availed yourselves of thus far, that you have no major problems in that respect. Could we hear from the Defence and have matters clarified, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yes, it is true that two days ago the Defence team of General Hadzihasanovic has been given access to confidential documents from the Kordic case, and today the Defence team of Brigadier Kubura has been informed that the documents from the Kordic case are also available to his Defence team. So to all intents and purposes, we can start using the documents today. I apologise, Mr. President, but I'd like to say, with regard to access to other documents, that the Defence is still waiting for confidential documents from the Naletilic and Martinovic case. As far as we have been informed, the last order was issued to the Defence teams of Martinovic and Naletilic that by December 2003 they should request additional protective measures for those documents, which means that our Defence teams will be able to have them ten to 15 days after that date and will be able to review those documents too after that date. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Are there any other questions that the Prosecution or the Defence wish to raise? I think that we have gone through all the other questions and items. Some have been resolved, others I hope are being resolved. But would the Prosecution like to raise any other matters at this stage? No, nothing?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Would the Defence like to raise any issues? Mr. Bourgon has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have three topics we would like to inform you of today. The first with regard to the admissibility of testimony in two cases, in the Blaskic trial and another one; and the second subject has to do with procedure to be followed with respect to the Prosecution evidence and exhibits to be supplied to the Defence teams before trial; and the third subject has to be -- has to do with a recent request made by the Prosecutor, that is to say a motion, ex parte motion, for a subpoena to be issued for a particular witness the identity of which has not been disclosed. As to the first question, the admissibility of testimony by the two accused, the two accused, that is to say General Hadzihasanovic and Kubura, have both testified in the case Prosecutor versus Blaskic. Now, in both cases, these accused were witnesses who were called by the Chamber pursuant to Article 88 of the Rules of Evidence and Procedure. And the accused Hadzihasanovic also testified in another case, that is to say the Prosecutor versus Krstic, at that trial, and also in that case they were called by the Trial Chamber pursuant to Rule 88. The accused Hadzihasanovic also has in the past made a declaration available to the Prosecutor, a statement to him. And the Defence received information from the Prosecutor that they would be using those documents during the Prosecution case. On the first -- in the first instance, the Defence referred to those documents in its motion, pre-trial motion, and in that Defence pre-trial motion, we indicated our intentions to oppose the use of those documents and previous declarations and statements. Since then, the Prosecution has sent in their expert report, the report of the expert they wish to call. They say they will do so in the month of January. So we have received that. And there is the 30-day time limit which allows us to make our comments with respect to the report and that this should be done by the 26th of November. The expert will be using prior testimony by the two accused, and we feel that with respect to what we have been told, that the Prosecutor will also be referring to the prior testimony given by the two accused in their opening statement. Consequently, representatives of the two accused intend to file a motion with the Chamber to the effect that these documents, that is the previous testimony of the two accused as well as the statement given to the Prosecutor by the accused Hadzihasanovic, should not be used in the course of this trial. Since we are going to file this motion very shortly, we would like to ask you, Mr. President, to render an order to the Prosecution not to refer to those prior statements, not to give those documents to the Chamber until a ruling is made regarding our motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Regarding your opposition to the production by -- let me first address myself to the Defence and I will give you the floor afterwards. What is your legal basis for opposing -- on which grounds are you opposing the use of the testimony in the Blaskic case or written statement given by your client to the Prosecutor? What are the legal grounds for you to ask the Prosecution not to use that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The legal basis regarding our motion that is going to be filed can be found in Article 21 of the Statute, the rights of the accused, the rights regarding presumption of innocence, so that the accused does not have to make a statement before the Chamber. The accused did testify in the Blaskic case on the same facts which will be judged by this Chamber, and on that occasion these two accused were not informed of their right to keep silent and to avoid self-incrimination. That is the principle legal basis for our motion. Of course, there are other legal motives on which our motion will be based. That is Article 92 bis (D) of the Rules, which envisages reference to the use of the testimony of an accused in another trial. But we have also other motives for this motion based on comparative law and national systems which do not allow for the use of previous statements of an accused in his trial and to see whether these accused testified as witnesses, as accused, or were forced to testify. And those provisions do not provide for the use of such testimony when those accused are on trial. We are going to submit this motion in writing, indicating clearly the grounds which should allow that testimony not to be used as well as statements during trial, and I think it is important for us to say that this is a matter of principle that goes to the very core of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you intend to table this motion in writing, but when do you intend to file it? Because as you know, the trial begins on Monday [as interpreted] at 9.00 a.m., and it should normally begin with the opening statement. When do you intend to file your motion? Because as you know, a motion, once filed, first requires the Prosecutor to respond to it in writing. So there will be a problem of time, because the trial is beginning at 9.00 a.m. on Tuesday. Also regarding the arguments that you have offered regarding the opening statement which the Prosecution will be making, as you know, in comparative law the Prosecutor is free to say what he thinks orally, and therefore you are raising the problem of limiting the right of speech of the Prosecutor in a statement which is only an opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We fully take note of your statement. Regarding the opening statement of the Prosecutor, we quite agree with you that the opening statement is not part of the record of the evidence, and the Prosecutor is free to discuss what he intends to submit as evidence. But if a Chamber needs to make a decision that a certain document cannot be used, it would be opportune for good understanding between the two parties for that not to be referred to. Of course we will be guided by your ruling in that respect. Regarding the question of when the motion will be filed, the report of the expert has been in our hands since Wednesday, and we will file the motion as quickly as possible, which means that if this motion has an impact on a ruling that you may make regarding the opening statement, we can file it already on Monday. If, Mr. President, you feel that it is not necessary for the Chamber to make any ruling before the opening statement, then again our motion will be filed as soon as possible but not necessarily on Monday. What is important for us, Mr. President, is, as soon as possible, that is at the Pre-Trial Conference, to notify the Chamber of our intention, as we did in our pre-trial brief, that we oppose the admissibility of the testimony of the two accused in the Blaskic case and the statement given by Hadzihasanovic to the Prosecutor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to the Prosecution to respond on this particular point, the Prosecution has understood that we find ourselves in time constraints, and if the Defence files a motion Monday, Tuesday, or Wednesday regarding the admissibility of evidence, the only urgent issue is that if in your opening statement you refer expressly to the object which is contained in the statement previously, then there could be a problem. So we have realised the legal impact of the motion, that is to prevent a witness who -- a witness who testified in another trial and who was not informed at the time that that testimony may one day be used against him. So the question that needs to be addressed is whether in your opening statement you intend to refer to this as this is the problem that the Defence is raising. The Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We can answer that quite simply. The Prosecution does not intend to refer to the prior testimony of Mr. Hadzihasanovic or Mr. Kubura in its opening statement. The Prosecution submits -- I'm not arguing the point now, but submits that the prior testimony is relevant, probative and admissible. The Defence has been on notice since we filed our pre-trial brief on October the 10th that we intended to use that evidence in -- at trial. They have had since October the 10th to file a moment in limine to determine the issue before trial. They have not done so. The Prosecution of course accepts that there are some reasonably complicated issues of law involved here and there is a mixture of approaches from common law and civil systems and, as Mr. Bourgon points out, there is jurisprudence which may go either way. The Prosecution will, of course, argue the matter properly when the time comes. As Mr. Bourgon points out, the Prosecution expert, General Rheinhardt, has referred to and relied upon parts of the previous testimony of Mr. Kubura and Mr. Hadzihasanovic in his report. As Mr. Withopf said earlier, he won't be giving his evidence until late January. If the Trial Chamber were to make a ruling against the Prosecution, it could be excised from his report. The Prosecution does not anticipate that it will come close to tendering or attempting to tender that evidence or the annexes to General Rheinhardt's report until sometime in January. The Prosecution considers it premature to discuss this issue at the moment, and we'll, of course, file a motion with considered legal argument when the time comes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will close on that point. It appears already that in the opening statement of the Prosecution on Monday [as interpreted], there will be no reference to that testimony. So this should satisfy the Defence. So there's no urgency that this motion has to be filed in the -- as soon as possible, because the question will arise only when we come to the testimony of the expert witness in January. So you will have plenty of time to draft that motion. As it is now 12.35, in view of technical problems and the need for a rest, we will have a short 15-minute break to address the two other points that you raised, and that is the procedure to be applied regarding inculpatory evidence and the motion of the Prosecution. We will have a 15-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. The hearing is resumed after this brief break. We are now going to address the two other points raised -- just a moment. Let us wait for the accused. I was saying that we're going to address the two last issues raised by the Defence that have to do with the procedure to be followed for Prosecution Exhibits, and the second point, the filing of a motion by the Prosecution. I give the floor once again to Mr. Bourgon who raised these issues. You have the floor. Or to Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Just briefly to deal with this matter that we raised, and it has to do with the ex parte request for subpoena. We are quite clear that in keeping with Rule 54, each party can ask for a subpoena to be issued, and we didn't see any problems in that regard. However, the question arises as to why this subpoena was asked for ex parte, because usually a subpoena can be treated within Rule 69, within the framework of various protective measures being accorded. But also, the identity of an individual must be disclosed to the Defence on time for the Defence to be able to prepare for cross-examination. I should like to inform you, Mr. President, that during the break we discussed the matter with our colleagues from the Prosecution, and they told us what they did and gave us certain guidelines. They said there was no problem for their part in disclosing to us the reasons which guided them in turn. So I think that after this discussion we had during the break, we have no requests or motions to make of the Trial Chamber on that score. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So if I understand correctly, following the conversation that you had during the break, you are no longer raising the problem. So the question has been resolved. Very well. The last point, and that is the procedure regarding Prosecution exhibits. What is the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It is a question of a practical nature but also of a legal nature. We were informed that all the documents on the list of the Prosecution documents will be given to the Chamber on an informal basis at the beginning of the trial, and following the last Status Conference, it was also agreed that some three weeks in advance the Prosecutor would disclose the -- would serve the statement of witnesses who would be heard in the next three weeks. The Prosecutor has already started to apply this mechanism, and it has communicated to the Chamber the statements of future witnesses for two particular incidents, that is the witnesses that will be called to testify about Dusina and those who will be testifying about Miletici. So the practical matter appears to have been regulated regarding the procedure. However, the Defence would like to draw your attention to the potential danger of such a practice when the trial begins. We have been told that this practice has now been established before the International Criminal Tribunal, that it is current practice that all the documents and statements are given to the Chamber before the witnesses are heard and before those documents have been admitted into evidence. We also know that there's a ruling of the Appeals Chamber on this subject, and though it doesn't specifically deal with this question, it says that it is possible for the Judges to see the testimony in advance and to see the documents in advance. I would just like to draw your attention this morning to the potential danger of such a procedure. As you probably know, Mr. President, that within an Anglo-Saxon system as soon as a Judge sees a document, before it is admitted into evidence, or if a Judge sees a witness statement before hearing that witness, that is sufficient to annul the process as a whole. Of course we are not applying the Anglo-Saxon system. You know also that in the continental law system, the Judge will see at the beginning of the trial what is known as "the file," but there is a distinction to be made between the file received by a Judge in the continental law system and the documents served on the Chamber in this system. Because in the former case, what the Judge receives is a file of the documents that are of the Prosecution and of the Defence. So those -- in this case, however, the documents provided to the Chamber are only the incriminating documents. Let me give you an example. If all the documents are given to the Chamber and the Judge consults those documents, it is quite possible that in the course of the trial the admissibility of a document may be called in question and the Chamber may even rule that it is not admissible. The same applies to the question of authenticity or another document which, by agreement between the parties, will no longer be fight filed, but the Judge has already seen them in advance. The Appeals Chamber has already ruled on this subject, but we would like to draw the attention of the Judges of this Chamber to the possibly prejudicial nature of such a procedure to the extent to which that the Chamber sees only the Prosecution documents, which could be prejudicial for the accused. Having said that, once the documents are provided to the Chamber, what is important from the point of view of the Defence is that all documents given to the Chamber should also be given to the Defence. And even if documents are doubled, even if they may be documents that we have already received on the basis of disclosures under Rule 66 or 68, if a document is provided to the Chamber, it should also be provided to the defence so that at all points in time the Defence knows which are the documents in the possession of the Chamber to avoid all confusion in the course of the trial, and then the Prosecution may refer to a document which the Chamber has in its possession and we may not. You know that such a situation did occur in certain cases before, and in order to avoid all possible confusion during the trial, we would like to ask that each document given to the Chamber in electronic or paper form should also be provided to the Defence. That is out of precaution. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I give the floor to the Prosecution now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the practice that has been established at Your Honour's request is the following: That the Prosecution provides Chambers with copies of the OTP statements of such witnesses it intends to call within three week's time. Chambers has been given such copies of witness statements, Defence has been informed the very same day such copies have been provided to Chambers. This issue has been addressed by Defence repeatedly. It is the understanding of the Prosecution that Chambers, that the Judges can certainly distinguish between the witness statement and between the evidence which will be the oral testimony of the witnesses in trial. In addition, I wish to say that pursuant to the ICTY Rules of Procedure and Evidence 65 ter (E)(ii), the Chamber gets the summaries of such witness statements anyway, and quite often there is not much of a difference, or not a huge difference, between the summaries on the contents, the relevant contents of such witness statement itself. Professional Judges, as we have here at this Tribunal, can certainly distinguish between the witness statement and the oral evidence. In respect to documents, none of such documents have been given to the Trial Chamber. There is not such a request. We will tender documents on a crime base by crime base basis, at least for the first weeks of this trial. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On this important matter raised in law, it appears that there is a potential danger, according to the Defence, that the Judges, being familiar with a written statement, may have a conviction before the oral testimony. So this has to do with the witness statements. As for documents, the Defence also fears that the fact that a document that may be in the possession of the Judges prior to trial may, in their mind, have a certain value before even it has been examined in cross-examination. So that is what the Defence is telling us. The Prosecution is rightly telling us that regarding witnesses, anyway, according to the Rules of Procedure, these summaries of testimony can be quite long, and they may be almost as long as the written statement - there's nothing to prevent it - and to give the Judges the entire statement does not carry this potential risk. This question, which is very important and interesting, was resolved by a ruling of the Appeals Chamber, and this ruling that I referred to at a previous Status Conference allows Judges to have knowledge of those statements or exhibits prior to the trial. It was decided on the previous occasion, in order to satisfy the Defence, to communicate such statements only a few weeks in advance, as has been done. As for the exhibits, for the moment we do not have any exhibit. It would perhaps be desirable, if you insist in this position, to file a motion on the matter so as to allow the Chamber to respond in law. Or another solution of a practical nature that may be satisfactory for everyone, the mechanism could be as follows - this is just an idea, not a ruling or decision - the Prosecutor would first give to the Defence the documents it will refer to, and if the Defence is not opposed, then the Chamber could be told about them, and if the Defence opposes it, no communication. That could be one solution. But another solution could also be that there should be no communication. In that case, we will have to act in accordance with the decision that has already been made in a similar case. So are there any additional observations to be made?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. You have made several proposals that should guide us, and I think that this is acceptable to the Defence, the proposals you've made, that perhaps one or two days in advance that the Prosecution should inform the Defence which exhibits it will tender to the Trial Chamber, and if we have any separate reason or special reason not to have this sent on, then we could make that clear in writing. However, the second question that Mr. Bourgon raised and which we should like to hear your pronouncements on is the following: Would it be necessary - and it is our position that it would be advisable and necessary - for the documents that you are sent in by the Prosecution, that those same documents should be disclosed to us regardless of the fact that at an earlier stage it had perhaps provided us with those documents, so that we could be able to form the same list that the Trial Chamber has. We could make this same list up. So that was our intention. And not to have any misunderstandings at trial as to whether a document had been previously disclosed to the Defence or not. So our proposal is to have simultaneous disclosure to the Trial Chamber, to Your Honours, and to the Defence teams so as to -- us to be able to make a file, court file, for the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This procedure of communication from the Prosecution towards the Chamber can also apply to the Defence when the time comes for its presentation of evidence, can be used to its advantage. What applies to one party applies to the other too. And therefore, to prohibit such a system, that prohibition would also apply to you. So what the Defence is also suggesting is that the Prosecution, when communicating those documents, should simultaneously communicate them to the Defence. So what is the point of view of the Prosecution in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In the event - and I emphasise in the event - the Prosecution would communicate documents to the Trial Chamber prior to tendering them into evidence, the Defence would be informed, following the suggestion of the Presiding Judge. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If I understand you correctly, there is no objection on the part of the Prosecution. When it is communicating a document to the Chamber, that they will simultaneously do so to the Defence. Is that my understanding? And when the Defence case comes, then it will act in the same way. It will produce documents to the Chamber and to the Prosecution simultaneously. So we take note of that. And if there should be any problems in the future, there will also be time for the Defence to file a motion. Are there any other matters to be discussed? No?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: No thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In that case, the Pre-Trial Conference is thereby completed. We will all meet again next Tuesday at 9.00 a.m. And the accused will also be present on Tuesday at 9.00, as they have to follow in person these hearings -- this hearing which had to do with the preparation of their trial. So I declare the hearing closed.
